reasons: The excerpt describes this combined mega-menu variation: a bestsellers carousel at the top, icons, social proof, and non-money links moved below products.
It ties the variation to observed new visitors opening the mega menu and reports nearly $50,000 in incremental monthly revenue.
The warning is otherwise supported: the speaker says that, without active discounts, a visible discount box can prompt coupon searches, frustrating coupon-site experiences, and abandonment.
The candidate adds the unsupported frequency qualifier "often leave"; the excerpt says users can become fed up and leave, but gives no frequency.
The excerpt explicitly recommends labels such as bestsellers and new where products are displayed side by side.
It also explicitly says not to label every product and instead make a couple of products stand out.
The excerpt supports that Boom displayed prices on collection-page buttons and explains this choice in the context of Boom being a consumable repeat-purchase makeup product.

The candidate turns that case-specific result into advice for consumable products generally, while the excerpt expressly qualifies that the approach "doesn't work with every single product or or or niche." This material limitation should constrain the action rather than appear only as an unknown.
The excerpt explicitly directs mobile collection pages to show "2x two" and four products above the fold.
It also specifically rejects oversized hero sections, banners, and text blocks when they prevent products from being visible above the fold.

The excerpt explicitly states that collection pages should reduce decision-making and decision paralysis by directing users toward best sellers, new products, low-stock products, and trending products.
The excerpt explicitly reports that this mega-menu test produced nearly $50,000 in incremental monthly revenue for Ezra's brand.
The excerpt reports "$40,000 uh dollars in monthly revenue" immediately after describing the combined cart changes of removing the discount box and adding the trust policy bar.
The candidate appropriately does not attribute the result to the trust policy bar alone.
The excerpt describes the landing page as "five makeup tips for older women" in a listicle style.
The candidate appropriately avoids claiming that this phrase was definitively the page title.
The excerpt says the team used data to hypothesize, devise, and run the described test variation.
It does not specify the data type or hypothesis method, and the candidate preserves those as unknown.
The excerpt explicitly says that, after presenting products as bestsellers that other people were buying, more people were "fomoing" into those products.
The candidate appropriately leaves unspecified whether that reported behavior reflected clicks, purchases, or another measure.
The excerpt describes direct add-to-cart from the collection page as part of Boom's specific consumable, repeat-purchase flow after showing the price.

It expressly warns that this approach "doesn't work with every single product or or or niche." The candidate generalizes it to consumable repeat-purchase products without representing that limitation as an action constraint or exclusion.

source_limitations: The excerpt begins mid-thought and ends with an incomplete sentence after "So not all of the".
The material is an informal spoken transcript with transcription ambiguities, including the internally unclear description of whether the guarantee box was collapsed and the phrase "2x two".
Reported revenue and behavioral outcomes are speaker assertions from case studies; the excerpt provides no test design, control definition, sample size, statistical method, duration, or baseline.
Several monetary results do not identify currency, and some results do not clearly state whether they are incremental revenue, total revenue, profit, or another metric.
The excerpt itself limits at least the collection-page price/direct-add approach by stating that it does not work with every product or niche, but it does not identify the applicable boundaries.
